plotbb puts a small grammar of graphics on top of R's base graphics. It is not
a replacement for base graphics and not a reimplementation of ggplot2: a
`bbplot` is still drawn by `graphics::points()`, `lines()`, `rect()` and
`polygon()`, and any base call can still be used. What the grammar adds is a
way to say *what* a figure is made of — data, mappings, layers, scales, labels,
facets — and a set of rules that make those pieces combine predictably.

This release (0.3.0) unifies the scale and legend semantics: one trained scale
per aesthetic, shared by the layers and the legend, with separate `col` and
`fill` scales. The vignette is organised the way the grammar is meant to be
learned rather than the way the functions are exported. Every section states a rule, shows it in a
running example, and then says what the rule implies — including where it stops.
The reference at the end lists the layers, the aesthetics they map, and the
known limits, so that a future version can extend this document without
rewriting it.

A note on reading: every code block runs with the package as installed, in
order, on the same small set of data (`mtcars`, plus a few summaries built from
it). The object `p` is introduced once and reused — redefined once, in the
section on inheritance, to add a colour mapping — so later chunks can focus on
the component being discussed instead of re-stating the whole plot. Terms are
used in a fixed sense throughout: a **plot object** is the description returned
by `bbplot()`; a **component** is anything added with `+`; a **layer** is a
component that draws data; a **mapping** is an expression in `bb_aes()`; a
**constant** is a fixed value such as `col = "tomato"`. "Stable" means the
behaviour is documented and tested here; anything planned for a later release is
marked as such and is not written as if it already worked.

Some familiarity with base graphics is assumed — enough to know that `par()`
changes device state and that `points()` draws on top of whatever is already
there. The grammar does not hide those mechanics; it gives them a structure.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
r_libs <- Sys.getenv("R_LIBS")
if (nzchar(r_libs)) {
  libs <- strsplit(r_libs, .Platform$path.sep, fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  libs <- libs[nzchar(libs)]
  .libPaths(c(libs, .libPaths()))
}
library(plotbb)
library(aplot)
library(dplyr)
```

## The grammar in one page

A plot is a **plot object** plus a series of **components** added with `+`:

1. `bbplot(data, mapping)` creates the object: the data every layer can see and
   the mapping every layer can inherit.
2. Layers (`bb_point()`, `bb_line()`, `bb_bar()`, ...) are added to it. Each
   layer may bring its own `data` and `mapping`, and draws in the order it was
   added.
3. Non-layer components change the figure rather than draw data: labels,
   themes, scales, legends, facets and grid lines.

The separation matters. A layer is the only kind of component that consumes
data; everything else adjusts the canvas, the decorations or the mapping from
values to ink. That is why a scale can be added after the layer that uses it,
and why a theme does not need to know which layers exist. It also explains the
division of labour between `bbplot()` and the layers: `bbplot()` sets the
defaults, and each layer says what it contributes on top of them.

The plot object is a description, not a drawing. Nothing is rendered when the
object is built; it is drawn when you `print()` it (or at the end of an
expression in a document such as this one). This deferred drawing is what makes
it possible to add a scale after a layer and still have the layer use it. It is
also where the graphics parameters are restored: `print.bbplot()` snapshots
`par()`, draws, and restores the snapshot, so a `bbplot` never leaves the device
dirty — not even when a layer fails.

`+` is therefore deliberately narrow: it adds one component to one plot. It is
not a layout operator and does not merge two complete plots; for several plots
side by side, build them separately and arrange them with `aplot::plot_list()`
as the examples below do. Third-party packages can still extend the set of
components: implement `bbplot_add()` for your class and return the modified
plot.

```{r plotbb-minimal}
p <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp))
p + bb_point(pch = 19)
```

## Data and mapping

`bb_aes()` records *mappings*: expressions evaluated against the data, not
values computed now. `bb_aes(mpg, disp)` means "the columns `mpg` and `disp`",
and `bb_aes(mpg, log(disp))` works as well because the expression is evaluated
per layer, in the layer's data. The practical consequence is that a mapping is
portable: the same `bb_aes(mpg, disp)` can be inherited by a layer that brings a
different data frame, and it will resolve against that frame.

`bb_aes()` captures only the aesthetics you actually write. There is no
inheritance inside `bb_aes()` itself and no silent completion of missing
aesthetics: a layer that needs `x` and `y` but receives neither fails with a
message, instead of quietly plotting against an index. This is intentional —
the grammar is explicit about what is mapped rather than guessing.

```{r plotbb-mapping}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, log(disp), col = factor(cyl))) +
  bb_point(pch = 19)
```

A mapping can also refer to objects from the calling environment; it is not
restricted to columns of the data. The expression keeps the environment it was
written in, so a variable defined just before the plot is visible inside the
layer. This is convenient for thresholds and highlights, and it is also the
reason a mapping should not depend on objects that change after the plot is
built: the expression is evaluated when the plot is drawn, in the layer's data,
with that captured environment.

```{r plotbb-mapping-env}
highlight <- 300
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, col = disp > highlight)) +
  bb_point(pch = 19)
```

## Layers override the plot mapping

Every layer inherits the plot's `data` and `mapping`, and may override them.
The inheritance is per aesthetic, not per mapping object: a local mapping is
merged into the inherited one name by name. This is what lets a layer change the
colour while keeping the coordinates, and it is why the examples below write
`bb_aes(col = ...)` without repeating `x` and `y`.

* A local **mapping** overrides the global mapping **aesthetic by aesthetic**.
  `bb_point(bb_aes(col = factor(am)))` keeps the inherited `x` and `y` and
  replaces only `col`.
* A local **data** replaces the plot data for that layer and contributes to
  the axis ranges. When the layer data carries the facet variable, each
  `bb_facet_wrap()` panel takes the rows with that panel's value; row-aligned
  data with the same number of rows as the plot data follows the panel row
  positions instead.
* `inherit = FALSE` turns the inheritance off: the layer then uses only its own
  mapping. Its data still comes from the plot unless you pass `data`.

The asymmetry between mapping and data is deliberate. A mapping is the part of
the plot that changes how values become ink, so a layer that opts out should
state it completely; data is the part that says which observations exist, and a
layer that only wants to add an annotation should not have to copy the frame it
was already given. `data` defaults to inheritance, and only an explicit `data =`
replaces it.

```{r plotbb-override}
p <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, col = factor(cyl)))

a <- p + bb_point(pch = 19)                                  # inherit everything
b <- p + bb_point(bb_aes(col = factor(am)), pch = 19)        # override col only
c <- p + bb_point(bb_aes(mpg, disp), inherit = FALSE, pch = 19)  # no inheritance

plot_list(a, b, c, ncol = 3, tag_levels = "A")
```

A second data frame is a normal layer argument. Here the points come from the
plot data and the group means come from a summary that the layer brings itself;
the axis ranges cover both.

```{r plotbb-layer-data}
means <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarise(mpg = mean(mpg), disp = mean(disp), .groups = "drop")

bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) +
  bb_point(pch = 19, col = "grey60") +
  bb_point(bb_aes(mpg, disp), data = means, col = "firebrick", pch = 17, cex = 2)
```

With `inherit = FALSE` the layer has to state everything it draws. Leaving `x`
and `y` out is an error rather than a silent fallback to the global mapping,
because a layer that draws nothing is harder to diagnose than a layer that says
which mapping it is missing:

```{r plotbb-inherit-false}
#| error: true
p + bb_point(bb_aes(col = factor(am)), inherit = FALSE)
```

## Constants are not mappings

A mapping varies with the data; a constant does not. Both are written in the
layer call, but they mean different things, and the difference is the one most
often worth getting right. Think of a mapped aesthetic as a *question asked of
the data* ("which colour does this row get?") and a constant as a *parameter of
the pen* ("this layer is drawn in firebrick"). The first can be trained by a
scale and summarised in a legend; the second cannot, because there is nothing to
train.

* `bb_point(bb_aes(col = factor(cyl)))` — **mapped**: the colour follows the
  scale and the legend.
* `bb_point(col = "tomato")` — **constant**: the whole layer is one colour. It
  is not trained by a scale and is not repainted by one, even if the scale or
  the legend is added later in the `+` chain.

```{r plotbb-constant}
pal <- c(`4` = "#1b9e77", `6` = "#d95f02", `8` = "#7570b3")

mapped <- p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_scale_col_manual(pal)
constant <- p + bb_point(pch = 19, col = "firebrick") + bb_scale_col_manual(pal)

plot_list(mapped, constant, ncol = 2, tag_levels = "A")
```

When an aesthetic is both mapped and given as a constant on the same layer, the
constant wins. The constant is the more specific statement — it is written for
this layer, at this point in the call — while the mapping is a default that the
layer chose to override:

```{r plotbb-constant-wins}
p + bb_point(pch = 19, col = "tomato")
```

A constant does more than win the draw: it **removes the mapping of that
aesthetic for the layer**. The aesthetic is not trained by a scale, not redrawn
by a later scale, and — for the statistical layers — it does not group either.
The rule is applied once, before the layer is built, so every layer follows it.

Aesthetics that can be both mapped and fixed are `col`, `fill`, `pch`, `lty`,
`cex` and (for text) `label`. For a layer that draws one element per row, a
constant is either a single value or one value per drawn row; a row-aligned
constant follows the same rows as the data, so dropping rows with `NA` or
infinite coordinates never shifts it onto the wrong point. Any other length is
an error, not silently recycled.

```{r plotbb-constant-length}
#| error: true
p + bb_point(col = c("red", "blue"))
```

```{r plotbb-constant-aligned}
d <- data.frame(x = c(1, NA, 3), y = c(1, 2, 3))
bbplot(d, bb_aes(x, y)) +
  bb_point(col = c("red", "green", "blue"), pch = 19, cex = 2)
```

The second point is dropped, and the third keeps its own colour: the constant
vector is row-aligned, not recycled.

Summary layers are the exception, because their constants are graphical
parameters rather than row-level aesthetics: `bb_hist()` and `bb_density()` use
`col`/`fill` as the fill of the bars or polygon, and `bb_boxplot()`/`bb_bar()`
use `col` for one box or bar each. There a vector means one value per bar, box
or group, exactly as in the base function they wrap.

## Order of layers

Layers are drawn in the order they were added, so later layers sit on top.
Moving a layer in the chain changes what covers what, and nothing else. There is
no z-order attribute, no priority number and no automatic reordering: the `+`
chain *is* the drawing order. This is the base graphics model kept intact, and
it is the reason semi-transparent fills behave the way they do — two overlapping
polygons mix in the order they are drawn.

```{r plotbb-order}
points_then_fit <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) +
  bb_point(pch = 19, col = "grey50") +
  bb_lm(col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)

fit_then_points <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) +
  bb_lm(col = "firebrick", lwd = 2) +
  bb_point(pch = 19, col = "grey50")

plot_list(points_then_fit, fit_then_points, ncol = 2, tag_levels = "A")
```

## Components that are not layers

`+` also accepts components that change the figure instead of drawing data.
Most of them take effect when the component is added, so their position in the
chain is not significant; where order does matter it is stated explicitly. The
two notable cases are labels, which are last-one-wins, and scales, which are
read when the plot is drawn so the last scale for an aesthetic is the one in
effect. Themes are applied at the start of drawing, which is why a theme can be
added after the layers it affects.

```{r plotbb-components}
p +
  bb_grid(col = "grey85", lty = "dashed") +
  bb_point(pch = 19) +
  bb_labs(title = "mtcars", sub = "displacement versus mileage",
          xlab = "miles per gallon", ylab = "displacement") +
  bb_theme_minimal()
```

### Labels

`bb_labs()` sets several labels at once; `bb_title()`, `bb_sub()`, `bb_xlab()`
and `bb_ylab()` set one each. A later label replaces an earlier one for the same
element. Labels are not drawn by the layers: they are applied once, after the
layers, by the plot's print method, so they always sit above the data and cannot
be covered by a later layer.

### Theme

`bb_theme()` takes `graphics::par()` settings and applies them to this plot
only. A theme has no side effect on the device: it is applied when the plot is
drawn and the previous parameters are restored afterwards, also when a layer
fails. That is what makes predefined themes safe to reuse, and it is why the two
plots below can share a device without the first one's background leaking into
the second.

This behaviour is the difference between the grammar and calling `par()`
directly. `par()` is device state: it persists until something resets it, so a
plot that changes it affects whatever is drawn next. A theme is plot state: it
travels with the object, is applied inside the print method, and is undone
before control returns. If you find yourself wanting `par()` outside the plot,
the device-level themes below are the supported way to express it.

```{r plotbb-theme}
a <- p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_theme(bg = "lemonchiffon", mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1)) +
  bb_title("bb_theme()")
b <- p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_title("untouched device")
plot_list(a, b, ncol = 2, tag_levels = "A")
```

Presets are combinations of `bb_theme()` settings:

```{r plotbb-theme-presets}
a <- p + bb_point(pch = 19, cex = 1.6) + bb_theme_expand() + bb_theme_deepblue() +
  bb_title("bb_theme_deepblue()")
b <- p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_theme_minimal() + bb_title("bb_theme_minimal()")
c <- p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_theme_bw() + bb_title("bb_theme_bw()")
d <- p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_theme_grey() + bb_title("bb_theme_grey()")
plot_list(a, b, c, d, ncol = 2, tag_levels = "A")
```

### Device-level themes

When you want a theme to last beyond one plot, use `set_bb_theme()` and
`unset_bb_theme()`, or `with_bb_theme()` for a block of code. `with_bb_theme()`
restores the previous state even if the code fails, and can be nested: the
restoration is scoped to the block rather than to the whole session, so a failed
example does not leave the device in a different state than it found it.

```{r plotbb-with-theme}
with_bb_theme(bb_theme_deepblue(), {
  bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) + bb_point(pch = 19, cex = 1.6)
})
```

## Scales and legends

A scale turns a mapped aesthetic into ink. It is trained from the data the plot
draws, then used both by the layers and by the legend, so the two can never
disagree about what a value looks like.

### Training

Training happens when the plot is printed, not when a layer is added. It
collects the mapped values from the plot-level mapping and from every layer's
effective mapping — including layers that bring their own data — and stores the
result in the scale. Two consequences matter in practice:

* a scale works regardless of where it sits in the `+` chain, because all the
  layers have already been seen when it is trained;
* constants are removed from the mapping before training, so a constant colour
  never contributes a level to the scale or the legend.

Legends are automatic: every mapped aesthetic (`col`, `fill`, `pch`, `lty`,
`cex`) gets an outside legend unless `bbplot(auto_legend = FALSE)` or an explicit
`bb_legend()` component for that aesthetic takes over. The automatic legend for
a layer-local mapping is tied to that layer, so its title comes from the layer
mapping rather than the plot mapping. A free-colour facet skips automatic
outside legends because one legend cannot describe several colour domains.

Facets train once on the full plot and share the resulting domain by default:
the same value gets the same colour in every panel. `free_colour = TRUE` opts
into a per-panel col/fill domain (an explicit colour scale is required; the
default mapping is value-based and therefore identical across panels). A free
colour facet cannot use an outside legend, because one legend cannot describe
several domains.

### Discrete scales

For a discrete mapping, levels come from factor levels first (in factor order),
then from character values in first-appearance order. `drop = TRUE` (the default)
keeps only levels that occur in the data; `drop = FALSE` keeps all factor levels.
A named manual palette matches by name, an unnamed one maps in level order, and
a value that the scale does not cover maps to `na.value` with a warning instead
of being silently recycled.

```{r plotbb-scale-manual}
pal <- c(`4` = "#1b9e77", `6` = "#d95f02", `8` = "#7570b3")
p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_scale_col_manual(pal) + bb_legend()
```

`limits` restricts the trained domain: for a discrete scale it also defines
which levels are shown.

```{r plotbb-scale-limits}
p + bb_point(pch = 19) +
  bb_scale_col_manual(pal, limits = c("4", "6")) +
  bb_legend()
```

### Continuous scales

A continuous mapping interpolates between colours over a trained numeric domain.
`limits` fixes the domain; `oob = "squish"` (the default) clamps values outside
it, `oob = "censor"` maps them to `na.value`. A zero-width domain is widened by
half a unit, and an all-missing domain leaves every value at `na.value`.
`minor_breaks` adds small ticks between the labelled breaks of the colour bar.

```{r plotbb-scale-gradient}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, col = hp)) +
  bb_point(pch = 19) +
  bb_scale_col_gradient(low = "grey85", high = "firebrick") +
  bb_legend(title = "horsepower")
```

Breaks and labels are shared by the layer colours and the colour bar:

```{r plotbb-scale-breaks}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, col = hp)) +
  bb_point(pch = 19) +
  bb_scale_col_gradient(low = "grey85", high = "firebrick",
                        breaks = c(100, 200, 300),
                        labels = c("low", "mid", "high")) +
  bb_legend(title = "horsepower", orientation = "horizontal",
            position = "bottomright")
```

### Fill is its own aesthetic

`col` and `fill` are separate aesthetics with separate scales. A layer that maps
`fill` uses a fill scale if one is given and the default fill mapping otherwise;
it no longer borrows the `col` scale. This makes the rule explicit and removable
in one line: add a `bb_scale_fill_*()` scale.

```{r plotbb-scale-fill}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(factor(cyl), mpg, fill = factor(cyl))) +
  bb_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  bb_scale_fill_manual(c(`4` = "#1b9e77", `6` = "#d95f02", `8` = "#7570b3")) +
  bb_legend(aesthetic = "fill")
```

Other aesthetics have their own scales, and each legend names its aesthetic:

```{r plotbb-scale-aes}
a <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, col = factor(cyl), pch = factor(gear), cex = hp)) +
  bb_point() +
  bb_scale_cex_continuous(range = c(0.8, 2)) +
  bb_legend(aesthetic = "col", position = "topleft") +
  bb_legend(aesthetic = "pch", position = "bottomleft")

b <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, group = gear, col = factor(gear))) +
  bb_lm(lwd = 2) +
  bb_scale_col_manual(c(`3` = "#1b9e77", `4` = "#d95f02", `5` = "#7570b3")) +
  bb_legend(position = "topleft")

plot_list(a, b, ncol = 2, tag_levels = "A")
```

A mapped line type is drawn by the line-like layers, not only shown in the
legend:

```{r plotbb-scale-lty}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, group = gear, lty = factor(gear))) +
  bb_lm(lwd = 2) +
  bb_scale_lty_manual(c(`3` = "solid", `4` = "dashed", `5` = "dotted")) +
  bb_legend(aesthetic = "lty", position = "topleft")
```

### Legend placement

`bb_legend()` draws a discrete legend with `graphics::legend()` and a continuous
colour bar with a dedicated function; both read the same trained scale as the
layers. `orientation = "horizontal"` turns the colour bar, and `outside = TRUE`
moves any legend into a dedicated layout column so it cannot cover the data. In
a faceted plot an inside legend is repeated in each panel; `outside = TRUE`
draws it once for the whole figure.

```{r plotbb-legend-outside}
p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_legend(aesthetic = "col", outside = TRUE)
```

By default the legend describes the whole plot, through the plot-level mapping
and the shared scale. `bb_legend(layer = )` selects one layer's mapping and uses
its default title (`layer` is a 1-based index or a layer name); the colours
still come from the shared scale, so this selects the explained mapping, not a
second domain. `style = "bar"` turns a discrete col/fill legend into adjacent
colour blocks, and `title_width` wraps a long title.

```{r plotbb-legend-layer}
layer_data <- data.frame(
  x = 1:6, y = 1:6,
  g = factor(rep(c("a", "b"), 3)),
  h = factor(rep(c("u", "v", "w"), each = 2))
)
bbplot(layer_data, bb_aes(x, y, col = h)) +
  bb_point() +
  bb_line(bb_aes(group = g, col = g)) +
  bb_legend(layer = 2, title = "line grouping")
```

Free colour facets are an opt-in, not the default:

```{r plotbb-free-colour}
free_data <- data.frame(
  x = 1:6, y = 1:6,
  panel = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 3),
  g = factor(c("u", "v", "u", "v", "w", "w"))
)
bbplot(free_data, bb_aes(x, y, col = g)) +
  bb_point() +
  bb_scale_col_manual(c(u = "red", v = "blue", w = "green")) +
  bb_facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 2, free_colour = TRUE)
```

## Positional scales

The x and y axes have their own scales, separate from the aesthetic scales.
`bb_scale_x_continuous()` and `bb_scale_y_continuous()` take `limits`, `breaks`
and `labels`; `bb_scale_x_log10()`/`bb_scale_y_log10()` are log10 shortcuts, and
`bb_scale_x_date()`/`bb_scale_y_date()` use Date limits and
`graphics::axis.Date()`. Limits are the final axis range, so a point outside
them is clipped rather than stretching the canvas.

```{r plotbb-position}
pos_data <- data.frame(x = 1:20, y = seq(1, 100, length.out = 20))
bbplot(pos_data, bb_aes(x, y)) +
  bb_point() +
  bb_scale_x_continuous(limits = c(5, 15),
                        breaks = c(5, 10, 15),
                        labels = c("low", "mid", "high")) +
  bb_scale_y_log10(limits = c(1, 100))
```

A date axis keeps the Date class for its limits and breaks:

```{r plotbb-position-date}
date_data <- data.frame(date = as.Date("2024-01-01") + 0:20,
                        value = 1:21)
bbplot(date_data, bb_aes(date, value)) +
  bb_point() +
  bb_scale_x_date(format = "%b %d")
```

`bb_coord_flip()` swaps the axes, including the axis labels and positional
scales. It is deliberately limited to coordinate-symmetric layers (`bb_point()`,
`bb_line()`, `bb_text()`, `bb_segment()`, `bb_tile()`, custom layers and
`bb_hline()`/`bb_vline()`); a layer that computes its own orientation (violin,
boxplot, bar, density, histogram, ribbon, smooth, lm, errorbar) raises an error
instead of drawing sideways.

```{r plotbb-coord-flip}
bbplot(pos_data, bb_aes(x, y)) +
  bb_point() +
  bb_hline(50) +
  bb_coord_flip()
```

## Facets

`bb_facet_wrap()` splits the plot into panels by a formula. The formula is
evaluated against the plot data to produce a panel key per row; the panels are
the sorted unique keys. Because each panel draws the same plot object with a
subset of the data, the layers, their order, and their constants apply unchanged
inside every panel — faceting changes which rows a panel sees, not how a panel
is drawn.

Layer data follows the panels: each panel takes the rows of the layer data that
carry the panel's facet value. Row-aligned layer data with the same number of
rows as the plot data falls back to the panel row positions, and a layer with no
rows in a panel is simply absent from that panel. Data that has neither the
facet variable nor the same row count cannot be split, so it is drawn in every
panel and the plot warns instead of failing silently. The three cases are worth
keeping in mind when a layer brings its own summary: giving it the facet column
is always the safest option.

The formula is evaluated as an expression. The same expression is reused on each
layer's data, so a combined or transformed key behaves the same for the plot data
and for a layer that brings its own rows.

```{r plotbb-facet}
p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_facet_wrap(~cyl, ncol = 3)
```

By default all panels share one range, which makes the panels comparable. A
free scale computes the range per panel from that panel's data (including layer
data), which makes each panel use its space fully but hides differences in
level. The choice is a reading decision, not a cosmetic one; the grammar only
provides the switch.

```{r plotbb-facet-free}
p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_facet_wrap(~am, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y")
```

Because the facet is an ordinary expression, a combined key needs no special
syntax:

```{r plotbb-facet-multi}
p + bb_point(pch = 19) +
  bb_facet_wrap(~paste(cyl, am, sep = "/"), ncol = 2)
```

Unused factor levels are dropped by default. `drop = FALSE` keeps them as empty
panels, which makes a missing group visible instead of silently absent; an
empty panel uses the global limits even on free scales. `labeller` changes the
strip text and `strip_width` wraps a long strip, with the top margin following
the wrapped number of lines.

```{r plotbb-facet-drop}
facet_data <- data.frame(
  x = 1:6, y = 1:6,
  f = factor(rep(c("a", "b"), each = 3), levels = c("a", "b", "c"))
)
bbplot(facet_data, bb_aes(x, y)) + bb_point() +
  bb_facet_wrap(~f, ncol = 3, drop = FALSE,
                labeller = function(key) paste("group", key),
                strip_width = 10)
```

`bb_facet_grid()` puts one variable on rows and another on columns. Every
combination of row and column keys gets a panel; a combination without rows is
drawn empty. Column labels sit on top, row labels on the right. With free
scales, x is shared within a column and y within a row, matching the grid
reading order.

```{r plotbb-facet-grid}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) + bb_point() +
  bb_facet_grid(rows = ~cyl, cols = ~am)
```

## Statistical and annotation layers

The statistical layers take the same data and mapping arguments as the
geometric ones and contribute their own ranges. "Statistical" here means that
the layer computes something from the rows before drawing: a histogram bins a
numeric variable, a density estimates its distribution, a boxplot summarises it
by group, a fitted line estimates a trend, a violin estimates a distribution per group,
a smoother fits an explicit model, and `bb_signif()` draws comparisons.
There is no separate statistic API to learn — the summary is part of the layer,
and its result is what takes part in the ranges.

`bb_hist()` and `bb_density()` share one grouping rule with the other
statistical layers: an explicit `group` mapping wins, then a discrete `x`, then
`col`, then `fill`. A constant colour is never a grouping. The rule is stated once and used
both when drawing and when computing the range, so a grouped histogram is
scaled to the tallest single group rather than to the pooled counts.

Two consequences follow from summarising. First, a summary layer consumes rows,
not just coordinates, so `bb_hist()` needs one numeric variable and does not
accept the `y` of a scatter plot as a second dimension — the `y` is the variable
being summarised when `x` is discrete. Second, constants on a summary layer are
graphical parameters for the resulting bars, boxes or polygons rather than
row-level aesthetics, which is why they are documented separately from the
per-row layers.

```{r plotbb-stat-layers}
a <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(factor(cyl), mpg)) + bb_boxplot(col = "grey90")
b <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg)) + bb_hist(col = "grey80", border = "white")
c <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg)) + bb_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5)
d <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(factor(cyl), mpg, fill = factor(cyl))) +
  bb_density(alpha = 0.5) + bb_legend(aesthetic = "fill")
plot_list(a, b, c, d, ncol = 2, tag_levels = "A")
```

```{r plotbb-signif}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(factor(cyl), mpg)) +
  bb_boxplot(col = "grey90") +
  bb_signif(comparisons = list(c("4", "6"), c("4", "8")))
```

`bb_signif()` is the one layer whose "data" is not a variable but a set of
comparisons; it draws brackets above the data and extends the `y` range so they
are not clipped. Its aesthetics are constants (`col`, `cex`, `lty`, ...) rather
than mappings, because there is no per-row value to map.

`bb_violin()` estimates one density per group with `stats::density()` and scales
it to `width` in x units, so groups with different sample sizes stay comparable.
With `orientation = "horizontal"`, map the numeric values to `x` and the groups
to `y`; `bb_boxplot(orientation = "horizontal")` follows the same convention.
`bb_coord_flip()` turns a vertical violin/boxplot sideways as well.
`adjust` and `bw` control the bandwidth; `kernel`, `trim` and `n` are passed
through. The layer is vertical, a group needs at least two finite values with a
non-zero spread, and a constant group is skipped with a warning rather than
silently drawn as a flat line. With a numeric `x`, the group positions are the
numeric values; with a factor or character `x`, groups sit at 1, 2, 3, ... and
the axis shows those numeric positions.

```{r plotbb-violin}
set.seed(7)
violin_data <- data.frame(
  group = factor(rep(c("a", "b", "c"), c(30, 25, 20))),
  value = c(rnorm(30), rnorm(25, 2), rnorm(20, 4))
)
bbplot(violin_data, bb_aes(group, value)) +
  bb_violin(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5)
```

The horizontal form swaps the mapping rather than the drawing code:

```{r plotbb-violin-horizontal}
bbplot(violin_data, bb_aes(value, group)) +
  bb_violin(orientation = "horizontal", fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5)
```

`bb_smooth()` makes the fit explicit: `method` is `"loess"` or `"lm"`,
`formula` defaults to `y ~ x`, `method.args` carries span or other fitting
arguments, and `se`/`level` control the confidence band. Fits happen when the
layer is added, so redrawing does not re-fit; a group with too few points or
distinct x values falls back to a linear fit with a warning. The band uses
`fill` (or the curve colour at low alpha), and the curve uses `col`/`lty`/`lwd`.

```{r plotbb-smooth}
set.seed(8)
smooth_data <- data.frame(
  x = 1:60,
  y = sin((1:60) / 8) + rnorm(60, sd = 0.3),
  g = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 30)
)
bbplot(smooth_data, bb_aes(x = x, y = y, col = g)) +
  bb_point(pch = 19, cex = 0.6) +
  bb_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, level = 0.95) +
  bb_legend(title = "group")
```

Fitted lines, intervals and errors follow the same pattern: the layer computes
the summary and contributes both the summary and its uncertainty to the range.

```{r plotbb-lm-errorbar}
means <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarise(x = cyl[1], y = mean(disp), sd = sd(disp), .groups = "drop")

a <- bbplot(means, bb_aes(x, y)) +
  bb_line(col = "grey50") +
  bb_point(pch = 19, cex = 1.5) +
  bb_errorbar(bb_aes(ymin = y - sd, ymax = y + sd), width = 0.8)

b <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, group = cyl, col = factor(cyl))) +
  bb_point() +
  bb_lm(lwd = 2, se = TRUE)

plot_list(a, b, ncol = 2, tag_levels = "A")
```

## Bands and reference lines

Two workflows come up often enough to deserve their own layers: a band that
shows an interval around a line, and reference lines that mark thresholds.

`bb_ribbon()` draws the band between `ymin` and `ymax` along `x`. It follows the
layer contract: `x`, `ymin` and `ymax` are mapped from the layer's data, a
constant or mapped `fill` (or `col`) sets the interior, and `alpha` controls its
transparency. Within a group the points are sorted by `x`, a group needs at
least two points (smaller groups are skipped with a warning), and rows with a
missing or non-finite coordinate are dropped; a missing group warns as well.
The band contributes its three coordinates to the ranges, so it can extend the
canvas without a separate call.

```{r plotbb-ribbon}
fit <- lm(disp ~ mpg, data = mtcars)
grid <- data.frame(mpg = seq(min(mtcars$mpg), max(mtcars$mpg),
                             length.out = 50))
ci <- as.data.frame(predict(fit, newdata = grid, interval = "confidence"))
ci$mpg <- grid$mpg

bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) +
  bb_ribbon(bb_aes(x = mpg, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), data = ci,
            fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3) +
  bb_point(pch = 19, col = "grey40") +
  bb_lm(lwd = 1.5, se = FALSE, col = "firebrick")
```

With a mapped `fill` the band is drawn per group. The grouping rule is the same
one the summary layers use: an explicit `group` wins, otherwise `fill` decides.

```{r plotbb-ribbon-groups}
bands <- data.frame(
  x = rep(1:5, 2),
  lo = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) - 0.4,
  hi = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) + 0.4,
  g = factor(rep(c("a", "b"), each = 5))
)

bbplot(bands, bb_aes(x, fill = g)) +
  bb_ribbon(bb_aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.3)
```

`bb_hline()` and `bb_vline()` mark reference positions. The intercept is either
a constant or a mapping, so thresholds can come from the data; a mapped
intercept can also carry `col` and `lty` per line.

```{r plotbb-reference-lines}
thresholds <- data.frame(threshold = c(100, 300))

bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) +
  bb_point(pch = 19, col = "grey40") +
  bb_hline(mapping = bb_aes(yintercept = threshold), data = thresholds,
           lty = 2, col = "steelblue") +
  bb_vline(20, col = "firebrick", lty = 3)
```

By default a reference line does **not** change the axis range: a line at the
edge of the data should not silently stretch the canvas. `expand_limits = TRUE`
is the explicit opt-in when the intercept must be inside the visible range.

```{r plotbb-reference-expand}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) +
  bb_point(pch = 19, col = "grey40") +
  bb_hline(500, col = "grey50", lty = 2, expand_limits = TRUE)
```

## Heatmaps

`bb_tile()` draws one rectangle per row, positioned at the `x`/`y` coordinates
and filled with the `col` (or `fill`) aesthetic. It is the one geometric layer
where `fill` and `col` mean the same thing — both name the interior of the
rectangle — and it is the simplest way to see a continuous mapping with and
without a palette. Because each tile is independent, a scale applies per tile,
and a constant fills all of them the same way.

```{r plotbb-tile}
df <- expand.grid(x = 1:8, y = 1:6)
df$value <- with(df, x * y) + rnorm(nrow(df), sd = 3)

a <- bbplot(df, bb_aes(x, y, col = value)) + bb_tile() +
  bb_title("continuous mapping")
b <- bbplot(df, bb_aes(x, y, col = value)) +
  bb_tile() +
  bb_scale_col_palette("YlOrRd") +
  bb_title("with a palette")
c <- bbplot(df, bb_aes(x, y, col = value)) +
  bb_tile() +
  bb_text(bb_aes(label = round(value)), col = "black", cex = 0.7) +
  bb_theme_expand() +
  bb_title("with text labels")
plot_list(a, b, c, ncol = 3, tag_levels = "A")
```

## Writing your own layer

`bb_layer()` is the supported extension point. It takes a drawing function and
runs it inside the grammar: the function receives the resolved `x`/`y`, the
mapped aesthetics that were not overridden by a constant, and the fixed
aesthetics you pass in `...`.

The contract is the same one the built-in layers follow, and it is worth
spelling out because it determines what a custom layer can and cannot do:

* **data and mapping** are inherited from `bbplot()` unless the layer brings its
  own, and `inherit = FALSE` has the same meaning as elsewhere;
* **aesthetics** are resolved when the plot is drawn, so a scale added later
  still applies, and a constant wins over a mapping exactly as in the built-in
  layers;
* **drawing** happens in `+` order and receives the same rows that survived
  validation, with length-n constants already aligned to them;
* **errors** propagate unchanged: the drawing function is ordinary R code, and
  an error in it is reported as such, with the graphics state restored.

What the layer does not get for free is the part the built-in layers implement
for their own geometry: it does not extend the scales or the legend, and the
coordinates it computes itself (a band, a curve, a reference line) do not widen
the axes unless they are declared. Declaring them is what the second example
does.

```{r plotbb-custom-layer}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, col = factor(cyl))) +
  bb_layer(
    function(x, y, col, size = 1, ...) {
      graphics::points(x, y, col = col, pch = 19, cex = size)
      graphics::points(x, y, col = "black", pch = 1, cex = size)
    },
    size = 1.5,
    name = "hollow circles over points"
  ) +
  bb_legend()
```

A custom layer follows the rules of the grammar, and has the same limits:

* it inherits `data` and `mapping`, and accepts its own plus `inherit`;
* it is drawn in `+` order, and its errors propagate unchanged;
* it does **not** extend the scales or the legend automatically;
* coordinates it computes itself do not widen the axes unless they are declared
  with `limits`; mapped coordinates always count.

```{r plotbb-custom-layer-limits}
low <- subset(mtcars, mpg < 20)
p_low <- bbplot(low, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) + bb_point(pch = 19)
p_low +
  bb_layer(
    function(x, y, ...) graphics::abline(h = min(y) - 50, col = "firebrick", lty = 2),
    limits = list(y = c(min(low$disp) - 50, max(low$disp)))
  )
```

Without `limits`, the same line would be drawn below the canvas and clipped.

## The base graphics escape hatch

For code that is not worth wrapping, `+` also accepts a function, a formula or
an expression of base graphics calls. They are drawn in order, after the layers
added before them, and behave like any other layer with respect to graphics
state and error propagation. The difference between the three forms is only when
the code is evaluated: a function is called at drawing time, while a formula or
a quoted expression is evaluated when it is added, in the calling environment.
The formula form is convenient for one or two calls; anything that needs
arguments, loops or intermediate variables is clearer as `bb_layer()`.

These escape hatches are powerful and intentionally unvalidated. The grammar
does not know what a raw base call will draw, so it cannot contribute its
coordinates to the ranges, cannot tell whether it uses the data, and cannot
check its aesthetics. That is the trade: full access to base graphics, no
grammar guarantees. When the drawing should participate in ranges, facets or
scales, wrap it in `bb_layer()` and declare what it needs.

```{r plotbb-escape}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) +
  bb_point(pch = 19) +
  (~abline(stats::lm(disp ~ mpg, data = mtcars), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)) +
  (~text(30, 450, label = "base graphics still work", col = "steelblue"))
```

Existing plotting code can become the canvas itself with `as.bbplot()`. The
function you pass draws the background; layers, themes and labels are then
added on top of it. A canvas does not carry data, so a layer added to it must be
given `data =` explicitly — that is the one place where the usual inheritance of
data has nothing to inherit:

```{r plotbb-as-bbplot}
draw_background <- function() {
  plot(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$disp, pch = 19, col = "grey75",
       xlab = "", ylab = "")
  abline(stats::lm(disp ~ mpg, data = mtcars), col = "firebrick")
}

as.bbplot(draw_background) +
  bb_lm(bb_aes(mpg, disp), data = mtcars, lwd = 2, se = FALSE,
        col = "steelblue") +
  bb_title("a base plot turned into a bbplot") +
  bb_theme_minimal()
```

A third-party package can add its own component type by implementing
`bbplot_add()` for its class; the method receives the object and the plot and
must return the plot.

## Extending from a package

There are three levels at which code outside plotbb can join the grammar, and
they differ in how much of the grammar they get:

* **function / formula / expression** added with `+` is the raw base-graphics
  escape hatch. It draws in order and shares the graphics-state contract, but it
  is not validated, does not contribute to ranges and is not part of the scale
  or facet machinery. Use it for one-off additions.
* **`bb_layer()`** is the stable custom-layer entry point. It inherits data and
  mapping, honours constants, draws at print time in `+` order, follows the
  facets, contributes its mapped `x`/`y` (and any declared `limits`) to the
  ranges, and propagates errors unchanged. A statistical layer can also declare
  `aesthetics = "fill"`, `summary = TRUE` and a `range = function(plot, data,
  mapping)` returning `list(x = ..., y = ...)`, so it participates in ranges
  without editing package internals. It does not extend the scales or the
  legend.
* **`bbplot_add()`** lets a package define a new *kind of component*. A method
  receives the object and the plot, returns the modified plot, and should
  describe what to add rather than draw it — typically by calling the public
  `bb_layer()`. It must not draw directly, change the device or rely on internal
  helpers such as `build_layer()`; those are not part of the contract.
  Functions, formulas and expressions are fine as an escape hatch, but a
  package should register its component method with
  `S3method(bbplot_add, <class>)` in `NAMESPACE`.

```{r plotbb-third-party}
bb_threshold <- function(value) {
  structure(list(value = value), class = "bb_threshold")
}

bbplot_add.bb_threshold <- function(object, plot) {
  plot + bb_layer(function(x, y, ...) {
    graphics::abline(h = object$value, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
  })
}

p + bb_point(pch = 19) + bb_threshold(300)
```

The component is re-applied inside every facet panel, takes part in the `+`
order and is covered by the same graphics-state restoration as the built-in
components; the layer the method adds is not added a second time when a panel is
rebuilt.

Statistical grouping has one rule, exposed as `bb_group_values()`: an explicit
`group` mapping wins, then a discrete `x`, then a mapped `col`, then a mapped
`fill`. Custom statistical layers should call it instead of inventing their own
precedence.

```{r plotbb-custom-stat}
bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(factor(cyl), mpg)) +
  bb_layer(
    function(x, y, ...) {
      graphics::rect(0.5, min(y), 3.5, max(y), col = "grey95", border = NA)
      graphics::points(as.numeric(x), y, ...)
    },
    aesthetics = "fill",
    summary = TRUE,
    range = function(plot, data, mapping) {
      list(x = c(0.5, 3.5), y = range(data$mpg, na.rm = TRUE))
    }
  )
```

The custom drawing itself still follows the `bb_layer()` limits:
mapped coordinates count towards the ranges, coordinates it computes itself do
not unless declared with `limits`.

## Combining complete plots

`+` adds layers and components to **one** plot; it deliberately refuses a second
complete plot. Arranging several complete plots is a different operation and is
delegated to `aplot::plot_list()` from the same author's aplot package (aplot
has `plot_list()`, not `plot_grid()`):

```{r plotbb-aplot, eval=FALSE}
p1 <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp)) + bb_point()
p2 <- bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(hp, wt)) + bb_point(col = "firebrick")
aplot::plot_list(p1, p2)
```

This is not the same as `bb_facet_wrap()` or `bb_facet_grid()`: those split one
plot into panels, while `aplot::plot_list()` arranges separate plots. plotbb
keeps the two operations separate.

## A complete workflow

Putting the rules together: data, inherited mapping, a layer with its own data,
constants for the annotations, then labels, a scale, a legend and a theme.

Read the chain as a sequence of decisions. `bbplot()` fixes the data and the
default mapping, including the colour that will be scaled. The first `bb_point()`
inherits both and only adds a shape and a size, so the points follow the colour
mapping. The second `bb_point()` replaces the data but keeps the inherited
mapping, which is why the group means are positioned correctly and drawn as a
different shape without restating `x` and `y`. `bb_lm()` uses the same inherited
mapping to fit one line per colour group. The scale then translates the mapped
`cyl` values, and the legend names them; because both are added after the
layers, this is a compact demonstration of deferred drawing. Labels and theme
come last because they affect the frame rather than the data.

```{r plotbb-workflow}
means <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarise(mpg = mean(mpg), disp = mean(disp), .groups = "drop")

bbplot(mtcars, bb_aes(mpg, disp, col = factor(cyl))) +
  bb_point(pch = 19, cex = 0.8) +
  bb_point(bb_aes(mpg, disp), data = means, pch = 17, cex = 2.2) +
  bb_lm(lwd = 1.5, se = FALSE) +
  bb_scale_col_manual(c(`4` = "#1b9e77", `6` = "#d95f02", `8` = "#7570b3")) +
  bb_legend(title = "cylinders") +
  bb_labs(title = "mtcars", xlab = "miles per gallon", ylab = "displacement") +
  bb_theme_minimal()
```

## Inspecting and saving a plot

A plot object can be inspected without drawing it. `bb_build()` performs the
same computation the printer does — training the scales, resolving the
mappings, collecting the data and computing the limits — and returns a plain
list. It opens no device, changes no `par()` and does not touch the random
seed, so it is safe in tests and in batch code that only wants to check a plot
before rendering it.

```{r plotbb-build}
built <- bb_build(
  p + bb_point(pch = 19) +
    bb_scale_col_manual(c(`4` = "#1b9e77", `6` = "#d95f02", `8` = "#7570b3"))
)
names(built)
built$limits
built$layers[[1]]$name
built$scales$col$domain
```

Faceted plots report one entry per panel, with the limits that panel would use.
This is also where build and print are guaranteed to agree: both go through
`bb_prepare_plot()`, so the limits in the build result are the limits the
printer uses.

```{r plotbb-build-facet}
facet_built <- bb_build(
  p + bb_point() + bb_facet_wrap(~am, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y")
)
vapply(facet_built$panels, `[[`, "", "key")
facet_built$panels[[1]]$ylim
```

`bb_save()` writes a plot to a file. The device comes from the extension
(`pdf`, `png`, `jpeg`/`jpg`, `tiff`/`tif`, `svg`) or from an explicit `device`;
sizes are given with `units`, and raster devices take `res`. It closes only the
device it opened and restores the caller's active device, so it can be used
inside an existing graphics session.

```{r plotbb-save}
out <- tempfile(fileext = ".pdf")
bb_save(p + bb_point(pch = 19), out, width = 6, height = 4)
file.exists(out)
unlink(out)
```

An existing file is never overwritten unless `overwrite = TRUE`; a missing
directory, a device that conflicts with the extension and invalid sizes are
errors. On failure the temporary file is removed, the original error is kept,
the caller's device is restored and an existing target is left untouched (even
with `overwrite = TRUE`).

## The contract at a glance

The rules above, collected in one place. Each one is implemented once in the
package, tested, and used by every layer; the sections above show it in action.

1. **A plot is an object plus components.** `bbplot()` sets the data and the
   default mapping; `+` adds one component to one plot. Printing draws and
   restores the graphics state.
2. **Layers inherit `data` and `mapping`.** A local mapping overrides the
   inherited one aesthetic by aesthetic. `inherit = FALSE` removes the inherited
   mapping but keeps the inherited data unless `data` is given.
3. **Layer data is first-class.** It participates in the axis ranges and in
   `bb_facet_wrap()`; a panel takes the rows that carry its facet value,
   otherwise row-aligned data follows the panel positions, otherwise the plot
   warns and draws the layer unsplit.
4. **Constants win, and they remove the mapping.** A constant aesthetic is not
   trained by a scale, is not repainted by a later one, and does not group a
   statistical layer. Length-n constants are row-aligned and follow the rows
   that survive validation.
5. **Order is drawing order.** There is no other ordering; later layers cover
   earlier ones.
6. **Scales translate mappings at draw time, once per aesthetic.** A scale is
   trained from the plot and every layer, shared across facets, and used by both
   the layers and the legend. `col` and `fill` are separate; constants never go
   through a scale. A legend describes the plot-level mapping.
7. **Themes are plot state, not device state.** They are applied while drawing
   and restored afterwards, also on error. Device-level themes are explicit and
   scoped.
8. **Custom layers get the grammar, not the geometry.** `bb_layer()` inherits
   data and mapping, honours constants, draws in order and propagates errors.
   It must declare with `limits` the coordinates it computes itself, and it does
   not extend scales or legends.
9. **The escape hatches are unvalidated.** Functions, formulas and expressions
   draw in order and share the graphics-state contract, but they are not part of
   the range, scale or facet machinery.

## When something goes wrong

The error messages are written to point back at a rule. A short map:

* `requires data: supply it in bbplot() or through the layer's data argument` —
  the plot has no data to inherit, which is normal for a layer added to an
  `as.bbplot()` canvas. Pass `data =` to that layer.
* `has no data to draw` — the layer's mapping resolves to nothing. The usual
  causes are a missing `x`/`y` mapping, or `inherit = FALSE` without restating
  them.
* `has length N, but M row(s) were mapped` — a constant or mapping does not
  match the number of rows. The rule is length 1 or one value per row; there is
  no silent recycling.
* `has no finite coordinates to draw` — every row is `NA` or infinite after
  filtering. Dropping invalid rows is a rule, not an accident, so a layer with
  nothing left says so.
* `fill is not an aesthetic of this layer` — use `col`. `fill` only exists where
  the drawing primitive has an interior separate from its border.
* `does not carry the facet variable ... drawn in every panel` — a warning, not
  an error: give the layer data the facet column (or the same row count) if it
  should be split.
* `does not combine two complete plots` — `+` is not a layout operator; use
  `aplot::plot_list()`.
* a custom drawing is clipped — its coordinates are outside the canvas. Declare
  them with `limits = list(x = ..., y = ...)`.

## Reference

### Layers

| Layer | Requires | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bb_point()` | `x`, `y` | `position = "jitter"` with a reproducible `seed` |
| `bb_line()` | `x`, `y` | connects rows in data order |
| `bb_text()` | `x`, `y`, optional `label` | a constant `label` wins over a mapping |
| `bb_segment()` | `x`, `y`, `xend`, `yend` | `x1`/`y1` accepted as aliases |
| `bb_errorbar()` | `x` + `ymin`/`ymax`, or `y` + `xmin`/`xmax` | `orientation`, `width` |
| `bb_bar()` | `x` (`stat = "count"`) or `x`, `y` | vertical bars only |
| `bb_boxplot()` | `x`, `y` | groups by `x` |
| `bb_hist()` | numeric `x`, or discrete `x` with numeric `y` | For discrete `x`, draws comparable `y` histograms within each group; mapped colours are group-based |
| `bb_density()` | numeric `x`, or discrete `x` with numeric `y` | Grouped by discrete `x` or by `col`/`fill`/`group` |
| `bb_tile()` | `x`, `y`, `col` (or `fill`) | heatmap tiles |
| `bb_ribbon()` | `x`, `ymin`, `ymax` | sorted by `x`; `alpha`, `border`; one band per group |
| `bb_violin()` | `x` (group), numeric `y` | density per group; `width`, `adjust`, `bw`, `trim` |
| `bb_smooth()` | `x`, `y`, optional `group` | explicit `method`/`formula`; `se`, `level` |
| `bb_hline()` | `yintercept` or a `yintercept` mapping | no range change unless `expand_limits = TRUE` |
| `bb_vline()` | `xintercept` or a `xintercept` mapping | no range change unless `expand_limits = TRUE` |
| `bb_lm()` | `x`, `y`, optional `group` | `se`, `level` |
| `bb_signif()` | `comparisons`, or `xmin`/`xmax`/`y_position` | extends the y range |
| `bb_layer()` | a drawing function | your own layer; `limits` declares extra range |
| `bb_grid()` | — | `bg = TRUE` draws behind the data |

Each layer maps a defined set of aesthetics. Aesthetics outside this table can
still be passed as constants (they go straight to the base function) but are not
trained by a scale:

| Layer | Mapped aesthetics |
| --- | --- |
| `bb_point()` | `col`, `pch`, `cex` |
| `bb_line()` | `col`, `lty` |
| `bb_text()` | `col`, `label` |
| `bb_segment()` | `col`, `lty` |
| `bb_errorbar()` | `col`, `lty` |
| `bb_bar()` | `col` |
| `bb_boxplot()` | `col`, `lty` |
| `bb_hist()` | `col` |
| `bb_density()` | `col`, `fill` |
| `bb_tile()` | `col`, `fill` |
| `bb_ribbon()` | `col`, `fill` |
| `bb_violin()` | `col`, `fill` |
| `bb_smooth()` | `col`, `fill` |
| `bb_hline()` | `col`, `lty` (per line when the intercept is mapped) |
| `bb_vline()` | `col`, `lty` (per line when the intercept is mapped) |
| `bb_lm()` | `col`, `lty` |
| `bb_signif()` | none (constant `col` only) |
| `bb_layer()` | whatever the drawing function accepts (`col`, `fill`, `pch`, `lty`, `cex`, `label` are resolved) |

Workflow: `bb_build()` inspects a plot without drawing it; `bb_save()` writes
it to a device and restores the caller's device afterwards.

Extension: `bb_layer()` adds a drawing function inside the grammar;
`bbplot_add()` adds a new component class (register the S3 method in a package).

Position: `bb_scale_x_continuous()`, `bb_scale_y_continuous()`,
`bb_scale_x_log10()`, `bb_scale_y_log10()`, `bb_scale_x_date()`,
`bb_scale_y_date()`, `bb_coord_flip()`.

Components: `bb_facet_wrap()`, `bb_facet_grid()`, `bb_legend()`, `bb_labs()`
(and `bb_title()`,`bb_sub()`, `bb_xlab()`, `bb_ylab()`), `bb_theme()` with the presets
`bb_theme_expand()`, `bb_theme_grey()`, `bb_theme_deepblue()`,
`bb_theme_bw()`, `bb_theme_minimal()`, and the scales `bb_scale_col_palette()`,
`bb_scale_col_manual()`, `bb_scale_col_gradient()`, `bb_scale_fill_palette()`,
`bb_scale_fill_manual()`, `bb_scale_fill_gradient()`, `bb_scale_pch_manual()`,
`bb_scale_lty_manual()`, `bb_scale_cex_manual()`, `bb_scale_cex_continuous()`.

### Known limits

* `col` and `fill` have separate scales. A `fill` mapping without a fill scale
  uses the default fill mapping; it does not borrow the `col` scale.
* Mapped `lty` applies to the line-like layers (`bb_line()`, `bb_segment()`,
  `bb_errorbar()`, `bb_lm()` and `bb_boxplot()`). Layers without a line style
  (points, tiles, bars) take `lty` as a constant only.
* Facets share one trained colour domain; per-panel free colour scales are not
  supported.
* A custom layer contributes the ranges of its mapped `x`/`y` values and its
  `data` follows the facets. Coordinates it computes itself do not widen the
  axes unless declared with `limits`, and it does not extend the scales or the
  legend.
* `+` combines components of one plot; for several plots use
  `aplot::plot_list()`.
* `free_colour = TRUE` requires an explicit `bb_scale_col_*()`/`bb_scale_fill_*()`
  scale and cannot be combined with an outside legend. Without an explicit scale
  the default colour mapping is value-based and shared across panels.
* A per-layer legend selects the mapping/title of one layer but still uses the
  shared trained scale; it is not a second colour domain.
* `bb_violin()` and `bb_boxplot()` place groups at 1, 2, 3, ... and draw numeric
  axis labels there; the factor labels are not written under the positions.
* `bb_smooth()` accepts a formula whose response is exactly `y`; transform the
  data or the mapping rather than the response, so the band stays on the drawn
  scale.
* A mapped `col`/`lty` on `bb_line()` applies one value to the whole polyline; a
  polyline cannot change colour halfway. Add a `group` mapping to draw one line
  per group.
* `bb_coord_flip()` flips point/line/text/segment/tile/custom layers,
  violin/boxplot (toggling their orientation) and hline/vline; bar, density,
  histogram, ribbon, smooth, lm, errorbar and signif are not flipped.
* `bb_bar()` is vertical only; horizontal bars are not part of this release.
* Automatic legends are outside legends; a free-colour facet skips them because
  it cannot have one outside legend for several colour domains.
